intro: Guimaraes calls itself the birthplace of Portugal, and its oldest trees keep that history in a different register. Two plane trees below the Paco dos Duques predate the palace's 1930s reconstruction. An olive in the cathedral cloister carries the legend that named the city's patron, and eighteen camellias at the Palacio Vila Flor put Guimaraes on Portugal's Camellia Route. Up the Penha slope, past an undated monastery oak, the cable car's summit holds a Douglas fir and a giant eucalyptus, both recently classified. Out west, a stone pine with a crown wider than it is tall holds a roundabout.
meta_description: Eight classified trees in Guimaraes: an olive from a 1342 miracle, camellias on the Camellia Route, a monastery oak and two giants on Monte da Penha.
question_meta: Guimaraes' oldest tree by measured age is a camellia at the Palacio Vila Flor, planted around 1830. An undated monastery oak may well be older.
question_answer: Guimaraes' oldest tree by any published measurement is one of the eighteen camellias in the terraced gardens of the Palacio Vila Flor, planted around 1830 and measured at roughly 195 years in Portugal's tree register. Two plane trees below the Paco dos Duques, at about 165 years, and three Himalayan cedars at the municipal cemetery, around 115, are the next oldest confirmed ages here. One tree on this page is probably older than all of them and cannot be ranked: the oak at Santa Marinha da Costa, which the pousada's own guide calls several centuries old and which nobody has ever dated on its own. An olive in the cloister of Nossa Senhora da Oliveira carries the city's founding legend, dated to 1342, but no source ties that trunk to that year and the register records no age for it.
question_context: The camellias, the planes and the cedars all trace their ages to the same 2011 classification pass by Portugal's forestry institute, which is why they agree with each other to within a plausible margin. The camellias are worth the walk regardless of the number: Guimaraes and the wider Minho market themselves, with reason, along a Camellia Route, and eighteen trees on one estate is a collection rather than a curiosity. The oak at Santa Marinha da Costa is the interesting gap. Its trees were classified as a group in 1940, and the group's 290 years, measured in 2006, covers six species including a eucalyptus, which cannot have stood there that long, so the figure says nothing about the oak. The olive is the other open question. City tradition holds that a merchant set a crucifix beside a long-dead olive in the square in 1342 and that it turned green three days later, the miracle that named the church, the quarter and the city's coat of arms. The legend is well documented. That today's tree is the miracle tree is not, so the age is left open rather than implied.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Guimaraes?
faq.a: By measured age, one of the eighteen camellias in the gardens of the Palacio Vila Flor, planted around 1830. The oak at Santa Marinha da Costa is probably older, but nobody has ever dated it separately.

The first four, yes. The plane trees, the olive, the camellia garden and the cemetery cedars sit in and just outside the UNESCO centre, under three kilometres end to end. The monastery oak is a 25 minute climb east up the Costa slope, the Silvares pine is 4.5 km west on the city bus, and the Douglas fir and eucalyptus at Monte da Penha ride up together on the city's cable car, a separate outing to the mountain top.

faq.q: Do they cost anything to see?
faq.a: Almost none of them. The planes, the camellias, the cedars, the Silvares pine and the two trees on Monte da Penha all stand on open public ground, and the monastery gardens are open to visitors as well as hotel guests. The cable car up to Monte da Penha is a paid ride, though the summit itself has no gate or ticket. The one exception on the ground is the olive tree, reached through the cloister of the Museu de Alberto Sampaio for a one euro add-on to the museum ticket.

The olive in the cloister of Nossa Senhora da Oliveira. City tradition holds a merchant set a crucifix beside its long-dead trunk in 1342 and that it turned green again three days later, the miracle that gave the church, and this whole quarter of Guimaraes, its name.

trees.name: The Plane Trees of the Paco dos Duques

location.address: Jardins do Paco dos Duques de Braganca, Rua Conde D. Henrique, 4800-440 Guimaraes

trees.story: Most of what you see is younger than what grows beneath it. Building work on the Paco dos Duques began in 1420 for Afonso, illegitimate son of King Joao I and soon to be the first Duke of Braganza, and it was never finished. The palace slid into ruin after 1616, when Guimaraes itself was handed to a Spanish nobleman, and by the nineteenth century what was left housed an infantry barracks. The building tourists photograph today, with its steep slate roofs and half-timbered galleries, is largely a 1937 to 1959 reconstruction: the regime of the Estado Novo added two full floors to the front wing and a third to the sides, remaking a shell into the national monument it wanted Guimaraes, self-styled cradle of Portugal, to have. These two plane trees on the grassy slope below the walls predate that rebuild by decades. Measured at 150 years in 2011, they were already thick-trunked when the scaffolding went up. The larger, four and a half metres round, rises twenty-nine metres; its partner a few strides away is a size smaller, twenty-two metres tall. Stand between them and look up at the palace: the trees are the only part of the view that nobody had to reconstruct.
trees.access: Free, exterior lawn below the palace walls, outside the paid museum entrance
trees.transport: In the historic centre, on foot
trees.notes: Twin registration, about 20m apart; pin marks the larger tree (4.5m girth, 29m tall) over the smaller (22m tall). Age is the 2011 assessment (150y) carried forward. A CC BY-SA 3.0 photo pair exists on Wikimedia Commons (File:Q98443993.jpg, File:Q98443994.jpg, Vanbasten 23, 2021); File:Q98443994.jpg was viewed on 2026-08-07 and approved, an autumn frame with the castle behind and crown and trunk both readable.

trees.name: The Olive Tree of Nossa Senhora da Oliveira
trees.age_estimate: unknown, the register recorded no figure at its 2021 measurement

location.address: Claustro do Museu de Alberto Sampaio, Rua Alfredo Guimaraes, 4800-407 Guimaraes

trees.story: This tree gave the city its second name. According to the legend still told here, a merchant named Pero Esteves brought a crucifix back from Normandy in 1342 and set it beside an olive tree that stood dead in the square, its trunk long dried out. Three days later, so the story goes, the olive turned green again. Guimaraes called the miracle Our Lady's, and the collegiate church behind the square has been Nossa Senhora da Oliveira, Our Lady of the Olive Tree, ever since, with an olive branch worked into the city's own coat of arms. An older layer of the same legend pushes the planting back further still, to the Visigothic king Wamba and a cutting supposedly carried from the Garden of Olives in Jerusalem. What can be said honestly is narrower: the tree growing today in the church's Romanesque cloister, two metres ninety around the trunk, is not documented as that specific plant, and Portugal's tree register, which measured it last in 2021, recorded no age at all. Whatever its years, it stands exactly where the story says it should, in the cloister that once belonged to a monastery founded by Countess Mumadona Dias in 949, on the square that gave the church, and so this whole quarter of the city, its name.
trees.access: Paid, 1 euro cloister add-on to the Museu de Alberto Sampaio ticket, Tuesday to Sunday 10:00-18:00
trees.transport: In the historic centre, on foot
trees.notes: The legend is well documented and independently corroborated (church history, Wikipedia, city sources), but no source ties this specific trunk to the 1342 date or the Wamba legend, and the register itself gives no age. Published on the strength of the legend and the site, with the age question left explicitly open rather than implied.

best_time.label: September to November: the harvest, when the fruit turns from green to black

trees.name: The Camellias of Palacio Vila Flor

location.address: Jardins do Palacio Vila Flor, Av. D. Afonso Henriques 701, 4810-431 Guimaraes

trees.story: Eighteen camellias planted across two garden terraces here have outlived the building's most fashionable era by more than a century. The register puts them at around 195 years, planted in the 1830s, decades before the palace itself was extended into the grand house whose halls now show contemporary art. Camellia japonica arrived in Europe from East Asia in the eighteenth century as a hothouse curiosity for the wealthy; by the time these were planted it had become the flower a family used to say a garden mattered. Guimaraes and the wider Minho region took to it harder than most of Portugal, which is why the area still markets itself, without much exaggeration, along a Camellia Route. The eighteen trees here split into two groups on the lower and upper parterres of a three-terrace baroque garden, laid out with box hedges, stone fountains and a view back over the city; the garden won a national landscape architecture award in 2006. Camellias flower through the coldest months, January into March, when almost nothing else in a Portuguese garden is doing anything at all, which is presumably part of why a family planted eighteen of them and not one.
trees.access: Free, public garden, Monday to Saturday 09:00-13:00 and 14:30-20:00, Sunday 10:00-13:00 and 15:00-19:00
trees.transport: About 10 min walk from the historic centre, on Av. D. Afonso Henriques
trees.notes: Register lists the two parterres as separate entries (8 individuals lower, 10 upper) about 30m apart in the same garden; folded into one ensemble entry the way Setubal folds twin registrations. Pin marks the lower parterre; the upper is a short walk within the same grounds.

best_time.label: January to March, when the camellias flower and little else in the garden does

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedars of Atouguia Cemetery
trees.age_estimate: about 115 years (one of the three dated; see notes)

location.address: Cemiterio Municipal da Atouguia, Creixomil, 4835 Guimaraes

trees.story: Three Himalayan cedars stand at the gates of Guimaraes' municipal cemetery, tall enough that they read as a landmark from the road below rather than as cemetery planting. Cedrus deodara comes from the western Himalaya, from Afghanistan through to Nepal, where it can live past a thousand years and grow to twice the height these have reached; introduced to European parks in the nineteenth century, it became one of the standard conifers for an avenue meant to impress. One of the three, in the cemetery car park, was measured at 100 years old in 2011 and classified that June, with a trunk four metres seventeen around. Its two companions at the main entrance, girths of 4.10 and 4.47 metres, were added to the classification later and were never separately dated, though their size suggests the same generation rather than a younger planting. A cedar planted at a cemetery gate a century ago was a statement about permanence, evergreen and famously long-lived, standing over a place built for the opposite. It has mostly kept the promise: all three are alive and, unlike the graves around them, still growing.
trees.access: Free, public municipal cemetery, open during daytime visiting hours
trees.transport: About 20-25 min walk from the historic centre, or a short bus ride
trees.notes: Pin is the one dated tree (car park, classified Aviso no. 10, 17/06/2011). The other two, at the cemetery's main entrance about 200m away, carry an identical rounded coordinate in the register (a transcription artifact, not a literal single point) and were added to the public-interest listing in a later municipal candidatura without their own age figure. All three treated as one ensemble entry since they read as a single planted group at the same gate.

trees.name: The Oak of Santa Marinha da Costa

location.address: Cerca do Mosteiro de Santa Marinha da Costa, Pousada Mosteiro de Guimaraes, Largo Domingos Leite de Castro, Costa, 4810-011 Guimaraes

trees.access: Free. The gardens belong to the Pousada Mosteiro de Guimaraes, the hotel inside the former monastery, and the pousada describes its park as open to guests and visitors. No opening hours are published, so expect to walk in past a working hotel.
trees.transport: About 1.5 km east of the historic centre and uphill on the Costa slope, roughly 25 minutes on foot, or a short taxi ride
trees.how_to_recognise: The oak at the circular granite tank in the walled garden, crown thrown right across the water. Five other species share the 1940 classification here, so the tank is what tells you which tree you are under.
trees.story:
Nobody has put a number on this oak, and the official one is no help. Portugal's register classified the trees of Santa Marinha da Costa as a single group in 1940 and gives that group 290 years as measured in 2006, but the group is six species and one of them is a eucalyptus, a tree that did not reach Portugal until the nineteenth century. The figure describes a collection, not this trunk. The pousada's own botanical guide says only that the oak is several centuries old. That is as far as anyone has gone, so it is as far as this page goes. If you know better, tell us.

What it stands over is easier to state. A circular granite tank of the baroque period, ringed with stone seating and fed by a small watercourse, sits in the walled enclosure of a monastery that Augustinian canons held for some three hundred and fifty years before the Hieronymites took it in 1528 and ran a college there; by 1541 its degrees counted equal to Coimbra's. A fire in 1951 took the tiled panels along the friars' cells and the stone stair to the chapter room. The state bought the ruin in 1972, and Fernando Tavora spent the following decade turning it into a hotel, work that won Portugal's National Architecture Prize in 1987.

The oak is older than the hotel and older than the fire, and it puts the whole tank in shade. Beyond that, nobody has said.
verified_sources: https://si.icnf.pt/wfs/arv_class (process KNJ2/007, conjunto arboreo at the Pousada de Santa Marinha da Costa, classified D.G. no. 119, II Serie, 23/05/1940, 290 years across six species at the 2006 measurement)

https://www.pousadas.pt/pt/hotel/pousada-guimaraes/jardins-mosteiro (9 hectare park open to guests and visitors, the baroque circular tank, the carvalho-alvarinho several centuries old casting its crown over it)

https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosteiro_de_Santa_Marinha_da_Costa (Augustinian canons, the Hieronymites from 1528, degrees equated to Coimbra's by 1541, the 1951 fire, the state purchase in 1972 and Fernando Tavora's conversion, National Architecture Prize 1987)
trees.notes: Split out of the register's six-species conjunto (KNJ2/007) as a single collectible point: the oak at the baroque circular tank, which is the one tree the property's own botanical guide singles out and the one place in the park with an obvious spot to stand. Age deliberately left empty, the register's 290 years is a figure for the whole group and cannot be this trunk's, since the group includes a eucalyptus. Pin is the register's coordinate for the conjunto, not the tank, hence approximate. Access verdict 2026-08-14: the pousada's own gardens page says the park is for guests and visitors (hospedes e visitantes), which is the property stating its own access; no hours are published, so the access line says so.

best_time.label: August to September: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Stone Pine of Silvares

location.address: Rua 25 de Abril, rotunda da antiga E.R. 206, Silvares, 4835 Guimaraes

trees.access: Free, on a public roundabout, open at all hours
trees.transport: About 4.5 km west of the historic centre; Guimaraes city bus line 082, the Silvares to Pevidem circular, serves the village
trees.story:
This pine is as wide as it is tall and it stands in the middle of a roundabout. Portugal's register measures it at 26 metres high with a crown 26.4 metres across, on a trunk 3.8 metres round, held over a road junction on the old ER 206 in Silvares. It was 100 years old when the register measured it in 2011, which makes it about 115 now, and it was classified of public interest in June that year. Guimaraes municipality has exactly three stone pines with that status and this was the first.

Pinus pinea is the umbrella pine, the silhouette on every postcard of the Portuguese coast, and the shape is not decoration. It sheds its lower branches as it goes up and pushes everything sideways into a flat parasol on a bare column, a design for catching light above competitors rather than beside them. In a plantation it does this modestly. With light on every side, as here, it does it to the limit, which is how a tree ends up with a crown wider than it is tall.

It also drops pinhoes, the pine nuts that go into Portuguese Christmas cooking. The cones take three years on the branch before they open, which is a long wait for one afternoon of gathering.

There is no gate and no ticket here. There is a roundabout, and a hundred-year-old parasol standing in the middle of it.
verified_sources: https://si.icnf.pt/wfs/arv_class (process KNJ1/608, pinheiro-manso, Rua 25 de Abril, rotunda da antiga E.R. 206, Silvares, girth 3.8 m, height 26 m, crown 26.4 m, age 100 at the 2011 measurement, classified Aviso no. 9 of 17/06/2011)

https://www.cm-guimaraes.pt/areas-de-intervencao/urbanismo/patrimonio-e-bens-classificados/arvores-e-arvoredo-de-interesse-publico (municipal list of classified trees: three stone pines in the concelho, this one at Silvares on the antiga ER 206, classified 2011)
trees.notes: Pin is the register's rounded coordinate, so approximate, but the tree itself is unmistakable: the only large pine on the roundabout of the old ER 206 where it meets Rua 25 de Abril. Flagged because the girth, height and age all come from the ICNF register alone, with the municipal list as the second source for the classification rather than for the measurements. Age is the 2011 figure of 100 carried forward.

trees.name: The Douglas Fir of Monte da Penha

location.address: Monte da Penha, next to the Santuario de Nossa Senhora do Carmo da Penha, Costa, Guimaraes

trees.access: Free, open public ground on Monte da Penha next to the Santuario da Penha. No gate or ticket for the summit park itself.
trees.transport: Teleferico de Guimaraes (cable car) from the city centre, about 10 minutes for the 1.7 km ride, then a short walk to the sanctuary grounds; also reachable by road/car. Roughly 2.9 km from the historic centre as the crow flies.
trees.story:
Guimaraes' cable car climbs 1.7 kilometres up Monte da Penha in about ten minutes, and at the top, beside the art-deco sanctuary that gives the mountain its shrine, stands a Douglas fir nobody had separately catalogued until the city's own tree register caught up with it in 2021.

Two earlier passes at this site both missed it, folded by mistake into a huge, 790-specimen forest classification that covers most of Penha's woodland and cannot be visited as a single tree. This one is different: individually designated, its own case number, its own protection order. It measures 4.8 metres round and stands 35 metres tall, big enough that in 2022 it made the shortlist for Guimaraes' own Tree of the Year.

Douglas fir is native to the Pacific coast of North America, planted across Europe from the mid-1800s for timber and, on hilltops like this one, for the view a fast-growing conifer gives quickly. The register puts this specimen at roughly ninety years, though nobody has published the year it went into the ground, so treat the number as the register's own reading rather than a certainty.

Its neighbour, a giant eucalyptus a hundred and seventy metres away, shares the same summit and the same story: overlooked, then found. Together they make Monte da Penha two stops rather than one.

trees.name: The Giant Eucalyptus of Monte da Penha

location.address: Monte da Penha, near the Santuario de Nossa Senhora do Carmo da Penha, Costa, Guimaraes

trees.access: Free, open public ground on Monte da Penha. No gate or ticket for the summit park itself.
trees.transport: Teleferico de Guimaraes (cable car) from the city centre, about 10 minutes for the 1.7 km ride, then a short walk to the sanctuary grounds; also reachable by road/car. Roughly 2.9 km from the historic centre as the crow flies, about 170 m from the Douglas fir (gui_007 candidate).
trees.story:
Seven metres and five centimetres round at chest height, thirty-nine metres tall, a crown that spreads twenty-nine metres wide: the giant eucalyptus of Monte da Penha is built at a scale that makes the sanctuary beside it look modest.

The blue gum is not native to Portugal, brought from Australia in the nineteenth century for timber and now naturalised across the country's hillsides, but few individual specimens ever reach this size. When Portugal's forestry authority classified it as a tree of public interest in 2020, it drew a fifty-metre protection zone around the base, banning earthworks and excavation nearby, the kind of order usually reserved for a tree the authorities actively worry about losing.

It was already a landmark before the paperwork caught up. Press coverage from the classification describes it as a specimen admired by visitors to the Penha hills, and in 2022 it was shortlisted for Guimaraes' own Tree of the Year alongside the Douglas fir standing a hundred and seventy metres away, the other half of a summit that turns out to hold two record-scale trees rather than one.

Reach both by Guimaraes' cable car, a ten-minute ride up from the city centre, or by road.
